content: The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends routine vitamin A supplementation during pregnancy or lactation in regions where vitamin A deficiency is endemic, such as areas where night blindness is prevalent. This recommendation is based on the expectation that supplementation may improve maternal and newborn outcomes, including reducing mortality, morbidity, anemia, and infections. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effects of vitamin A supplementation, either alone or in combination with other vitamins and micronutrients, on maternal and newborn clinical outcomes. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized trials, including cluster-randomized trials, that assessed the impact of vitamin A supplementation in pregnant women. Data from 19 trials involving over 310,000 women were analyzed, while 15 trials were excluded, and one trial is ongoing. Seven trials were judged to have a low risk of bias, three had a high risk of bias, and nine had unclear risk. When vitamin A supplementation was compared to placebo or no treatment, the pooled results showed no significant effect on maternal mortality (risk ratio [RR] 0.88, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.65 to 1.20; high-quality evidence), perinatal mortality (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.07; high-quality evidence), neonatal mortality, stillbirth, neonatal anemia, preterm birth (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.01; high-quality evidence), or the risk of delivering a low birthweight baby. However, vitamin A supplementation was found to reduce the risk of maternal night blindness (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.98; two trials). There was also evidence suggesting that vitamin A supplementation may reduce maternal clinical infections (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.99; low-quality evidence) and maternal anemia (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.94; moderate-quality evidence). When vitamin A supplementation was compared to micronutrient supplements that did not include vitamin A, there was no reduction in maternal clinical infections (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.18; two trials, 591 women). No other primary or secondary outcomes were reported in this comparison. When vitamin A supplementation was combined with other micronutrients and compared to micronutrient supplements without vitamin A, there was no reduction in perinatal mortality (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.10 to 2.69; low-quality evidence), maternal anemia (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.09; low-quality evidence), maternal clinical infections (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.13; low-quality evidence), or preterm birth (RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.08 to 1.93; low-quality evidence). However, in HIV-positive women, vitamin A supplementation combined with other micronutrients was associated with a reduction in the number of low birthweight babies (<2.5 kg) in one study (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.96; one study, 594 women). The authors concluded that pooled results from three large trials conducted in Nepal, Ghana, and Bangladesh, involving over 153,500 women, do not currently support the use of antenatal vitamin A supplementation to reduce maternal or perinatal mortality. However, the populations studied likely differed in their baseline vitamin A status, and there were issues with follow-up in these trials. There is strong evidence that antenatal vitamin A supplementation reduces maternal night blindness and maternal anemia in women living in areas with endemic vitamin A deficiency or in HIV-positive women. Additionally, there is some evidence suggesting a reduction in maternal infections, but the quality of this data is low.
